articles.title: Alaska's GOP governor orders investigation into Peltola campaign after report
articles.summary: It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department last week sued in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Wednesday, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity. "I'm not naïve," he said. In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law. "Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections." Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2022, wrote in a statement that the people of her state deserve a full explanation. "Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments," she wrote. "By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong." Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. "Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation." Rep. James Comer, the Republican head of the House Oversight Committee, said Thursday that the committee is "taking action" to launch an investigation into the matter, including an inquiry into whether any crimes may have been committed. ABC News also reported Thursday that the DOJ had issued a wave of new subpoenas as it probes whether the alleged recruitment scheme may have run afoul of federal conspiracy laws. Yahoo The outcome of the legal dispute, if it moves forward, could have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a legal ruling that erases a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to this week's Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last week. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said Friday of the lawsuit . The suit argues that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats have asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, has also filed to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Monday, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Many legal experts say the lawsuit has a slim chance of success. First, it requires a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts say, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters does not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? The federal judge in Alaska considering Democrats' motion to dismiss the lawsuit i ssued an order late Wednesday allowing their challenge to move forward. She gave the DOJ until Thursday afternoon to respond. That likely only matters in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." articles.title: Google is on track for its worst day ever — with $500 billion in market value at stake
articles.summary: Alphabet ( GOOGL ) is on track for its worst day ever. The stock fell about 13% Thursday after its third quarter results , steeper than any session since it went public in 2004, including its drops in March 2020 and September 2008. At its low, Alphabet had lost $524 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Yahoo Finance Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It has already blown past the $400 billion SpaceX ( SPCX ) lost on June 22, the previous No. 2. In dollars, it's Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It's also on track for the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group . The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. Yahoo Finance The quarter gave both sides plenty to argue over. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, and the Gemini app passed 1 billion users. But search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion, short of Wall Street's roughly $65 billion estimate. Free cash flow — the cash left after paying for things like data centers — swung to a loss of about $9 billion as AI spending climbed. The company's stakes in AI labs cost it too. "The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business," Pivotal Research CEO Jeffrey Wlodarczak said in a rundown of why investors hated the quarter . CFRA's Angelo Zino was more patient, telling Yahoo Finance the pullback "probably represents a buying opportunity." Losses this size used to be unheard of. US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May. Yahoo Finance Amazon ( AMZN ) reports after Thursday's close, the last of the big three cloud providers to report this week. Faster growth at Amazon Web Services without a hit to cash flow would point to a problem specific to Google's search business. Another quarter of cash burn would put the whole AI spending trade back on the defensive. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. articles.title: Hegseth's treatment of lawmakers threatens Trump's $1.5 trillion defense plan
articles.summary: This summer, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asked a Republican lawmaker what he thought the odds were that Congress would pass the Trump administration’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request. The chances, the lawmaker responded, were about the same as Hegseth getting confirmed again by the Senate. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “You have a problem, and you need to increase the amount and the quality of the communication” with Congress, the Republican lawmaker recounted in an interview, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe the private exchange. Months later, members of both parties said the Pentagon has not changed course. For decades, defense issues have mostly remained insulated from Washington’s toxic partisanship. But Republicans and Democrats say they increasingly fear that fire wall no longer exists. With just over 20 legislative days left in the year - and next week’s election likely to empower Democrats eager to confront Hegseth - lawmakers are deadlocked on their major defense policy and spending bills. Failure would leave the Pentagon with few options to replace the thousands of weapons spent during eight months of war with Iran and halt the administration’s ambitious military agenda. To understand how the consensus collapsed, The Washington Post spoke with 30 people at the center of national security in Congress, including 20 lawmakers who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon and its budget. Republicans argued that Democrats are stalling critical military funding to placate voters incensed at President Donald Trump. Democrats framed their opposition as a necessary check on an administration that the GOP-controlled House and Senate have refused to hold accountable for starting a war without the approval of Congress. But most lawmakers who spoke with The Post described the impasse in more personal terms. Hegseth’s adversarial behavior - from withholding information to attacking Democrats and some Republicans - was straining the bipartisan dealmaking that has long ensured support for the military, members of both parties said. “The people who have been around for a few days have seen what normal looks like,” Rep. Joe Courtney (D-Connecticut) said. “We’re not living in normal.” In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Joel Valdez defended Hegseth’s approach, saying the secretary is “always willing to engage directly with any lawmakers who bring forward their concerns in good faith.” “Lawmakers understand exactly how critical the National Defense Authorization Act and defense appropriations are to military readiness,” Valdez said, referring to the pending bills. “We do not expect them to deliberately cripple the force or our warfighting capability simply to score political points.” The collapse of bipartisanship The NDAA is widely considered a must-pass bill. The legislation, which covers issues from troop pay to weapons production, has advanced for 65 consecutive years. A similar, albeit less reliable, coalition helps pass the annual defense spending bill, which provides the money to pay troops, buy weapons and conduct military operations worldwide. The group of Republicans and Democrats who typically support the legislation has fractured this year. The NDAA failed to advance in the Senate and barely passed the House, where more Republicans voted against it than Democrats voted for it. The two chambers are negotiating a final version with votes expected later this fall. At greater risk of failing, most lawmakers said, is the annual defense budget. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion plan would fund a range of advanced weaponry, from commercial-style drones to precision missiles depleted during the Iran war. It would direct billions more toward some of Trump’s personal projects for the military, including a Golden Dome missile defense shield, a fleet of battleships named after him and a renaming of the Defense Department as the “War Department.” Hegseth has called the 40 percent increase in spending an “urgent, necessary injection of resources” to outpace America’s adversaries. He has also urged Congress to approve an additional $67 billion in funding to help cover the costs of the Iran war and other military operations around the world. Nearly all Senate Democrats blocked the request in an extraordinary act of protesting the conflict. In a move that has frustrated some Republicans, the administration split the defense budget into two buckets: $1.15 trillion that will require some Democratic support and another $350 billion meant to pass with GOP votes alone. Republicans have so far failed to agree on a strategy to pass the party-line share of funding. The gridlock has left the military vulnerable, lawmakers said. U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, estimated that as of mid-October the Iran conflict had cost more than $47 billion, forcing the Pentagon to delay trainings and maintenance projects just to cover its bills. After failing to reach a lasting ceasefire this summer, the president has threatened to restart strikes after the midterms. “Russia and China are questioning whether or not we have the resources and the ability to quickly replace dwindling stocks and ammunition,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), who faulted Democrats for holding up the defense budget. “You’re mad at the president, but you’re taking it out on these men and women who are following orders.” Excluding the Democrats Democrats say the Trump administration is blaming them for problems of its own making. “To come in and say, ‘Oh, by the way, we made this choice and we spent all this money and we need you to replenish it’ - it takes a lot of nerve,” said Sen. Angus King (Maine), an independent who caucuses with Democrats. The Trump administration has excluded Democrats from several briefings on the $350 billion in defense spending it hopes to pass on a party-line vote. These meetings have broken a long-standing practice of sharing national security information equally with each party, lawmakers said. Multiple Republicans noted that the administration has tightened the briefings in part because of concerns about leaks to the news media, which Trump officials have blamed on congressional Democrats. Many in the GOP said they had urged the Pentagon to include both parties. “If we are asking them to make these country-altering decisions, I think we have to inform them,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (North Dakota), one of multiple Republicans who noted they’d urged the Pentagon to share more information with Democrats. The Republican lawmaker who offered Hegseth his blunt assessment of the $1.5 trillion request also said that Democrats are partly to blame for the lack of communication. Earlier this year, the lawmaker said, he brokered a private meeting between Hegseth and a small group of Democrats. All of the Democrats declined to meet with the secretary, the lawmaker said. Other members of Congress faulted Hegseth for the distrust. In April, while appearing before the House Armed Services Committee, Hegseth delivered a broadside in his opening remarks. “The biggest adversary we face at this point,” he said, “are the reckless, feckless and defeatist words of congressional Democrats and some Republicans.” At one point during the hearing, Rep. Austin Scott (Georgia), a senior Republican on the committee, noted that the administration would need Republican and Democratic votes to secure its budget. “The way Hegseth treats people is a problem,” Scott said in an interview. ‘Shockingly unprofessional’ During Hegseth’s first private meeting with the Senate Armed Services Committee, in June 2025, he opened with a warning, according to three people familiar with his remarks. Though the hearing was classified, the secretary said, he didn’t know - and didn’t trust - everyone in the room and would watch what he said, these people recalled. They cited the exchange as an example of Hegseth’s combativeness. “It’s as shockingly unprofessional as anything I see,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who voted against Hegseth’s confirmation and has opposed the Iran war, said of the secretary’s tone. Current and former officials familiar with Hegseth’s relationships on Capitol Hill disputed assertions that the Pentagon was withholding information from Congress or refusing to meet with Democrats. They said Hegseth’s private meetings had been professional and noted that Democrats had openly attacked him, accusing him of mismanagement and dishonesty. The Pentagon did not directly address questions about this encounter or others detailed in this report. The contentious relationship has led some Republicans to ask the Pentagon to instead send uniformed officers to brief Congress, lawmakers said. Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has hosted private breakfasts with Republicans and Democrats at the Pentagon in an attempt to build more bipartisan support for the budget, according to lawmakers and others familiar with the sessions. A spokesperson for Caine declined to comment. Meanwhile, members of both parties voiced a sense of resignation that the defense-related committees were becoming more partisan. “Democrats don’t want to work on anything in a bipartisan way that could be construed as giving Trump a win,” said Sen. Deb Fischer (Nebraska), a senior Republican. Many Democrats said they are worried that the Pentagon’s shortfalls could hamstring military readiness for years, including in a future Democratic administration. But they argued that they need to use every tool they have to resist what they see as an unconstitutional war. “We are taking serious risks with our national security and should not be,” said Sen. Chris Coons (Delaware), the top Democrat on the Senate panel on defense spending. “At the end of the day, the president’s responsible for the decisions he’s made.” Multiple people familiar with the budget negotiations, some speaking on the condition of anonymity to provide their candid assessment, said that the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion request was probably impossible with so little time left in the year. A U.S. official familiar with Hegseth’s relationships with lawmakers asserted that the full budget request was still viable and that Republicans, if they lose control of Congress, would see this as their last chance to secure defense-related priorities without Democratic votes. Doubts about the budget have come at a low point for Hegseth’s standing with congressional Republicans, who have signaled they will oppose his preferred picks to lead the Army and criticized him more openly in recent weeks. When the House returns in November, Hegseth will probably face an impeachment vote, led by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky), over the Iran war. Meanwhile, some Democrats felt emboldened heading into next week’s election - they appear likely to at least regain control of the House - and the prospect of launching aggressive oversight of the Pentagon. Earlier this year, Hegseth held private breakfasts with the top Republicans and Democrats on the Armed Services committees, in an effort to improve his standing. Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the House Armed Services Committee’s top Democrat, recalled saying near the end of his meeting with Hegseth that, despite their disagreements, they didn’t have to be enemies. In an interview, Smith said he wasn’t looking to partner with “this Pentagon.” “I’m looking,” he added, “for ways to stop the awful things they’re doing with our military.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/29/inside-breakdown-trumps-15-trillion-pentagon-plan/

articles.title: GOP poll suggests Ramaswamy's ad with rival's estranged mom is backfiring
articles.summary: A  campaign ad in which the estranged mother of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton argues that her daughter should not be elected as the Buckeye State's next governor has added a new level of controversy to what was already one of the most closely watched races of the midterms — and potentially shifted the course of the race in its final weeks. Acton, a Democrat, is running to replace outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. She's facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a billionaire who ran an unsuccessful presidential campaign in 2024. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur , calls her daughter a "liar" and urges Ohioans not to support her. "Don't let her become your governor," she says. "If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse." As the ad began to spread across social media on Oct. 20, Acton's brother released a statement in which he accused Arthur of siding with their stepfather after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was a child, and criticized Ramaswamy for attempting to use the alleged abuse as a "political talking point." Ramaswamy defended the ad, telling reporters that Acton's account of her past "does deserve to be scrutinized." His campaign confirmed to the Enquirer that it will spend $4 million to air the ad across the state. The ongoing controversy over the ad, which has been widely condemned by Democrats and sparked pushback from some Republicans, has put a new spotlight on the race for Ohio's top elected office. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, an incumbent Republican locked in a tight reelection race, released a statement saying he personally "would not have run" the ad. Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance, himself a former senator from Ohio, said Republicans who disapprove of the ad should " stop whining " and remember that politics is a "tough business" during a campaign stop in Cincinnati. DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy in the race, made his first public comments on the ad on Oct. 22, telling reporters that it was "wrong." "The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling, but when you know the rest of the story … it just makes it more wrong," he said. "It's wrong to run this ad." Trump weighed in on the controversy that same day, praising Arthur for her "courage." "What she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice!" He wrote on Truth Social. "The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good! Who wouldn't use such an Ad? I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'" Yahoo The opinions that really matter, though, are those of voters. It's too early to know the full scope of the ad's impact on the race, but the limited data available suggests the ad may be turning Ohioans away from Ramaswamy.  According to internal Republican polling reviewed by Axios , the ad is "having a significant effect on the gubernatorial race" and has led to a 2-percentage-point increase in Acton's lead. In a separate poll from Suffolk University , 72% of likely voters said they had seen or heard about the ad, but less than 0.3% said it had convinced them to back Ramaswamy. By contrast, nearly 2% said the ad had caused them to switch their support to Acton. In the same poll, about half of the respondents said Ramaswamy had run a more negative campaign, compared to 15% who said the same about Acton. Once a key swing state, Ohio has steadily become redder in recent decades. Four years ago, DeWine won reelection by more than 25 percentage points . But polls suggest that Acton has a chance to break the GOP's long run of control over the Ohio Statehouse. Here's what you need to know about who she is, how her past informs what she stands for today and what the polls say about her chances of winning. Who is Amy Acton? Acton has been open about the "difficult" childhood she endured growing up in Youngstown, Ohio, in the 1970s. On her campaign website, she says she overcame "periods of abuse, hunger, and neglect, and even wound up living in a tent in the middle of winter." In 2019, she publicly alleged for the first time that she had been sexually assaulted by her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, between the ages of 9 and 12. After Acton's biological father reported the alleged abuse in 1978, Arthur was arrested and charged with rape, according to contemporary news reports and court documents obtained by the Associated Press . Acton's mother sided with her stepfather, disputing the allegations. The couple left the state before Arthur could face trial and reportedly remained together until his death in 2004 . Both Acton and her mother say they have not seen or spoken to each other since a court hearing in which Acton testified against her stepfather nearly 50 years ago. "In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton told the now-shuttered newspaper the Vindicator in 2019. Arthur has had some difficult years since she and her daughter became estranged, according to court records obtained by NBC News . She was charged with theft in 1995, and she declared bankruptcy in 2011. More recently, she's faced multiple citations for animal neglect, including in 2021, when several kittens were found locked in her car on a hot day — one of them died. That case went to trial, and she was found guilty of animal neglect. The conviction was later overturned when an appeals court found she had been improperly denied a court-appointed attorney, according to NBC News. Acton found more stability after moving in with her father and became a standout student in high school. She earned a bachelor's degree from Youngstown State University and a medical degree from the Northeast Ohio School of Medicine, working various jobs to pay her way through college. She completed residencies in pediatrics and preventive medicine before becoming a professor at Ohio State University , where she taught classes on maternal and child health. She also directed a community organization called Project L.O.V.E. to promote preventive health care among Columbus-area children. In 2019, DeWine tapped her to become director of the Ohio Department of Health. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit a year later, she advised DeWine to take swift action to control the spread of the virus. Under her guidance, Ohio became the first state in the nation to shut down all public schools. Acton also gained national attention thanks to the daily public briefings she gave throughout the early stages of the pandemic. In May 2020, an opinion piece in the New York Times called her "The Leader We Wish We All Had." Acton resigned a month later amid pressure from the Republican-led state legislature to sign orders rolling back COVID restrictions, moves she would later say "there was no science for." She briefly remained part of DeWine's administration as a public health adviser before leaving to resume working in the nonprofit sector. She announced her plans to run for governor in early 2025 and cruised through the Democratic primary in May. Acton was married to her first husband, with whom she had three children, for nearly 20 years before they divorced in 2008. She married her current husband in 2010 and became stepmother to his three children. What does Acton stand for? As a Democrat running in a conservative-leaning state, Acton fits firmly into the moderate wing of her party. Her policy platform focuses heavily on affordability, including proposals to lower the cost of health care, combat fraud, cut high energy bills and crack down on corporations that take advantage of workers and consumers. In July, she drew criticism from some progressive Democrats for saying that she supported barring transgender children from participating in girls' and women's sports. Soon afterward, she added language to her website pledging to protect Ohio's LGBTQ community, without directly contradicting her previously stated stance on transgender athletes' participation in sports. Acton has also spoken in favor of Ohio's voter ID requirements, a position that puts her at odds with many Democrats who view such laws as a voter suppression tactic by Republicans. Acton has also called for an increase in funding for police departments, more money for public schools and heavy investment in Ohio's rural and farming communities. What are her chances? Polling in the Ohio governor's race has fluctuated significantly as Election Day has grown closer. In the aggregate, the polls suggest that Acton has steadily widened her lead over Ramaswamy in recent weeks. At the same time, two polls released in October show Ramaswamy ahead. The Cook Political Report and the Center for Politics , two of the country's top nonpartisan forecasters, list the race as a toss-up. articles.title: 'Operation Ghostbusters': DOJ unveils crackdown on student aid fraud scheme
articles.summary: The Department of Justice announced a sprawling operation seeking to end an elaborate student aid fraud scheme that authorities say has bilked potentially hundreds of millions of dollars from taxpayers. The effort, dubbed “Operation Ghostbusters ,” aims to crack down on an international fraud scam that has funneled stolen federal student aid dollars into offshore accounts since at least 2021. At an Oct. 29 news conference, Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald described the scheme, detailing how suspects steal Americans’ identities before applying to universities, receiving federal student aid and running off with the money. McDonald said perpetrators are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create so-called “ghost students,” filling out college applications and even completing coursework. Some fraudsters go as far as creating “the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present,” he said. “These are not isolated errors. This is organized fraud at scale," McDonald said, adding that taxpayer losses could potentially reach "several hundred million dollars." In California alone, one-third of community college applications submitted in 2024 were reportedly flagged as fraudulent, McDonald said. Heith Janke, assistant director of the FBI's criminal division, said the agency has so far identified more than $32 million in losses, with millions more suspected, in similar student aid schemes. "This stops now," Janke said in a statement. "The FBI, working hand-in-hand with our partners at the Department of Education and Department of Justice will follow all evidence, track every dollar, and pursue each criminal who seeks to exploit our nation’s systems.” The government’s expansive investigation involves 26 FBI field offices and more than 20 U.S. attorney’s offices, according to the DOJ. There are at least 40 open cases related to the scam. McDonald said the operation, which began in April, has so far led to charges against five people and the seizure of more than $750,000 in crypto currency tied to networks in Kenya. The defendants have been indicted in multiple states, including Nebraska and New Jersey. McDonald said the first round of charges is “just the beginning." “If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build their future, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said. articles.title: Obama-era investigation found evidence against Ilhan Omar's marriage, report says
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images) Federal investigators found evidence during the Obama administration suggesting that Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to a man suspected of being her brother was intended to help him obtain a green card, but the case stalled chiefly because prosecutors concluded the suspected offense fell outside a five-year statute of limitations, according to a new report. The FBI and Department of Homeland Security investigated the marriage in the summer of 2016, current and former officials told The New York Times in a report published Thursday. The officials' account challenges Omar's characterization of the earlier inquiry as having debunked allegations that she married her brother to help him obtain a green card. The newspaper said it remains unclear what evidence investigators had establishing that Omar and her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, are siblings. Marrying a person to help them obtain a green card is illegal under federal law, while marrying a sibling is illegal under state law. However, the newspaper noted that it remains unclear whether federal prosecutors could pursue charges against Omar despite the statute of limitations for marriage-based immigration fraud. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegations about her and her ex-husband. "Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," spokeswoman Jackie Rogers said in a statement. "This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump's failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress." Six current and former officials familiar with the 2016 investigation told the Times that agents found evidence suggesting Omar and Elmi were siblings. The officials said investigators had limited tools to develop the case because prosecutors did not pursue it. Omar was already a U.S. citizen when she married Elmi, a British citizen, in 2009. They divorced in 2017. Two former officials said Elmi obtained a conditional two-year green card through the marriage. When immigration authorities requested additional evidence before granting him permanent status without conditions, he left the United States and abandoned his petition, they said. The earlier inquiry involved an FBI agent specializing in public corruption and civil rights cases and two Homeland Security Investigations agents, according to the report. The allegations surfaced publicly in 2016 as Omar campaigned for a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives. After a local television station reported that the U.S. attorney's office had opened an investigation, her campaign sought a letter from Andrew Luger, then the U.S. attorney for Minnesota. In the Aug. 22, 2016, letter, Luger wrote that "my office is not investigating, nor have we requested an investigation into Ms. Omar." Omar portrayed the letter as an exoneration that put to rest "flat-out falsehoods." Luger, however, told the Times last week that the letter "was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims." He said it was intended only to rebut an erroneous report that he had asked ICE to investigate Omar. Luger said federal agents could have been pursuing the matter without his knowledge and denied shielding Omar from scrutiny. The Trump administration has reopened scrutiny of the marriage as part of a broader investigation into the Omar family's immigration history. Federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home Oct. 12, weeks before she seeks a fifth term in the House. Investigators are also examining whether Omar's late father submitted false or incomplete information during the immigration process and whether Omar was too old to qualify for citizenship through him in 2000, the Times reported. Democrats have condemned the inquiry as political persecution and said the search violated Justice Department policy intended to prevent investigative actions from influencing elections. President Donald Trump repeated the allegation that Omar married her brother last week. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the broader investigation could lead to Omar's deportation if authorities establish that she should not have been admitted to the country. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: Partial Israeli election results indicate possible deadlock as Netanyahu alleges fraud
articles.summary: Israeli election authorities were still counting votes from Tuesday's parliamentary election on Thursday morning. But even with the vast majority of ballots counted, it remained unclear who will form the country's new government. Neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his prime challenger Gadi Eisenkot has an obvious course to secure a majority of seats in the Knesset, according to exit polls and partial results released by electoral authorities. As of Thursday, Israel's Central Election Committee said it had counted nearly 94% of votes. The partial results -- which are subject to some change as the rest of the votes are tallied -- indicated that Netanyahu's Likud party would win 26 seats, with Eisenkot's Yashar party on 21 seats. The CEC projected that Netanyahu's coalition was on course to secure 53 seats, slightly ahead of Eisenkot's bloc on 48 seats. Neither coalition was on course to achieve a 61-seat majority. Maya Levin,jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: This combination of pictures created on Oct. 28, 2026, shows Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot (L) addressing supporters at a rally in Tel Aviv and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressing his supporters at an election night rally in Jerusalem. Israel awaits election results as exit polls suggest close race for Netanyahu The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected by the CEC to take 19 seats. The last stage of vote counting is expected to end on Thursday afternoon or evening local time, the CEC said. The final results will not be published until Nov. 4. If the CEC projections hold true, the two coalitions led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot may need the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties to have any chance of a majority in the Knesset. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have previously ruled out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. In his post-election speech, Netanyahu suggested that any government that included Arab parties would "endanger Israel." Arab party leaders have indicated willingness to work with the anti-Netanyahu opposition. The Arab-led Joint List -- a collection of three parties which between them were on course to win 12 seats as of Wednesday -- said in a statement that they were ready for "political cooperation to oust the Netanyahu government." Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo - PHOTO: An Arab woman walks with a child next to a torn Likud party campaign ad featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. No clear winner yet after polls close in Israeli elections, exit polls indicate "The Joint List will work with all its strength to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are ready for political cooperation to establish an alternative government, which will present a true alternative and commit itself to a true change of the current government's racist policy," it said in a statement. Mansour Abbas, the leader of the United Arab List -- also known as Ra'am -- which was projected to win seven seats, said he had been in touch with representatives of both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot coalitions. As vote counting continued on Wednesday, Netanyahu alleged -- without providing any evidence -- that the election had been "stolen by Arab parties," claiming that Likud had gathered evidence of electoral fraud and submitted it to electoral, law enforcement and security bodies. Likud issued a statement claiming that "foreign entities" had interfered with the election by providing financial support to Arab parties. The party did not immediately provide any evidence to support its allegation. Opposition leaders condemned the prime minister's remarks, maintaining that the elections in Israel were free and fair and there was no evidence of election fraud. The Israeli police said they will investigate any credible allegations of wrongdoing. Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gestures to his supporters at the election night rally after the first exit polls were announced, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. Dean Livne, the acting director general of the CEC said on Wednesday that there was "no basis for allegations of election theft," as reported by Israel's Kan radio station. Eisenkot, meanwhile, said on Wednesday night that he had undertaken "a long day of meetings, conversations, and preparations to realize the will of the voter." "We are focused on the heavy task entrusted to us -- bringing change to Israel," he wrote in a post to X. ABC News' Nasser Atta and Joe Simonetti contributed to this report. articles.title: Speaker Johnson signals he will keep leading Republicans even if they lose the House
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress. Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the majority leader, and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a conservative icon, are both expected to launch bids to lead House Republicans if Democrats flip the chamber, according to GOP lawmakers, aides and strategists. But Johnson recently muddled the leadership landscape by signaling his intention to keep his spot atop the party even if Republicans are knocked out of power. Then on Monday, President Trump offered a glowing endorsement of Johnson’s leadership chops, sparking further speculation that Johnson might, in fact, buck historic trends and try to remain leader even from the minority. “Mike Johnson is a true friend, fighter, and WINNER,” Trump posted on social media, “and he has my Complete and Total endorsement for Re-Election.” “Thank you, President @realDonaldTrump!” Johnson responded. “The best is yet to come as we save America!” Much about the leadership race is expected to come into sharper focus after next Tuesday’s midterm elections. A Johnson spokesperson said the Speaker is “solely focused on protecting the majority,” noting that he “will campaign in 21 districts across 13 states between now and Election Day.” But many Republicans are skeptical, predicting Johnson will follow the example of past GOP Speakers — including Newt Gingrich (Ga.), Dennis Hastert (Ill.), Paul Ryan (Wis.) and Kevin McCarthy (Calif.) — who all left Capitol Hill in short order after losing the gavel. “I highly doubt that the Speaker will go for minority leader at this point,” a GOP aide said Wednesday. “I just don't see him having a desire. I don't think he's having a fun time as Speaker. I don't think he'd want to be minority leader.” Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) defied modern tradition in 2011, when she clung to the minority leader seat after the party was clobbered in the 2010 midterms. Pelosi would win the gavel back eight years later, but she’s been the exception. GOP strategist Amy Frederiksen said, “When you lose, and you're no longer Speaker …it's hard to go back to minority leader.” “There’s certainly a lot less trappings and a lot less power, and also the caucus just tends to kind of want to clean some house. Like members just see it as an opportunity to just switch things up, and so it's not that it hasn't happened, of course. Speaker Pelosi went to be the minority leader, so it isn't unprecedented,” Frederiksen said. “It wouldn't be historic in any kind of way, and it's very possible. But it is — I don't think it's as simple as him just deciding. I think that the caucus is going to really want to weigh in on things.” She added that Johnson was a “compromise candidate anyway” for Speaker. “We went through a couple, two, three, four different potential Speakers, including Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan, when he was finally chosen as Speaker, so I, you know, I just think that there is that,” she said. “It was sort of a bargain struck anyway for him to be Speaker.” Some Republicans predicted next year’s leadership roster will hinge on how the midterms play out. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the elections are shaping up to be a referendum on the president, whose historic unpopularity has created huge challenges for GOP candidates and made Democrats the favorite to control the House next year. Still, some Republicans believe that if Democrats win by a wide margin, Johnson will bear much of the blame, lose support within the conference and struggle to secure the votes needed to become minority leader, even if Trump wanted him there. “I would imagine there to be more of a push for someone else, just given that over, you know, a billion dollars has been spent on the midterms alone,” a second GOP staffer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill earlier this month. Although both Scalise and Jordan have downplayed their interest in the top spot, many Republicans say they’re both angling for the position, setting the stage for a potentially messy internal fight when House lawmakers return to Washington the week after the midterms. (Minnesota Rep. Tom Emmer, the Republican whip, says he wants to remain in that seat). There’s plenty of disagreement about who would have the advantage in such a race. Some say that if it’s a two-way race between Scalise and Jordan, Scalise would likely be better positioned than Jordan to step into the top spot given his current leadership position. “I think for Scalise … it'd be an easy transition for him to step into that. But for Jordan, he's really — how do I phrase this? He's been a loyal soldier. He's rallied people well, and he's an effective politician. So I think both would do well in the role, but I think Scalise would have an easier transition just out of pure — his House leadership currently,” a third GOP staffer said. The first Republican staffer, though, predicted Jordan has the edge. “He's done a lot of work over the past couple years where he's kind of built his own coalition, [and] he does have, like, a cult following around the country when he goes on the campaign trail. So I do think it's his to lose at this point,” the first aide said. “When you're in the minority, you need somebody who can be a fighter and willing to go out there and go on TV and bomb some bombs. And I think he's the guy for it.” The offices of Scalise and Jordan did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Johnson has faced a rocky tenure as Speaker, often marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference united on government spending, the Iran war and other issues. Even so, Johnson told CBS News’s Robert Costa this month that in the “unlikely scenario” Republicans lose the House, “I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.” “I’m going to continue to serve my highest best use to God and country, and I believe right now, as we’re sitting here, that’s the Speaker of the House,” Johnson said. “And if we lost the majority, I don’t think that that position that I have would change. I think I would stay right there.” Some Republicans note that if Johnson were to jump into the minority leader race, he would have a strong case for the position. The third GOP staffer noted Johnson’s “had to deal with a lot of curveballs” and that he’s handled them well. “I think that the party recognizes that and will react accordingly,” the staffer said. “That doesn't mean there's not people gunning for the same spot, but I think Johnson has been a good leader, a team player amidst what is, you know — we could say honestly — has been some chaos at times.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: The data center boom is facing a voter backlash as health concerns take hold
articles.summary: Page, Arizona — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health. "I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers." "There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said. Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction. The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections . The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building. Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes. It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds. "Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio. "That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending." The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI , with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend , an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists. Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies . Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside. Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals , synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing . Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands. "We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele , executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now." A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts. "Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition . It cuts across politics Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth. Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned. Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Mr. Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview , a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won. Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Mr. Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support. "This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in." In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards. The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely , who won his primary with an endorsement from Mr. Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new construction in their district. The House seat they're vying for is considered competitive, and the contest could be pivotal in determining which party gains House control after the Nov. 3 midterms. In Arizona, 57% of registered voters oppose construction of more large data centers, according to an August opt-in online poll of 1,040 registered voters by Noble Predictive Insights. More than costs Photos from across the nation featuring politicians at groundbreaking ceremonies for data centers held only a year or two ago are now campaign fodder. That has become a big problem for some elected leaders in Ohio, where more than a dozen local referendums or initiatives related to construction of the facilities will appear on ballots — the most of any state. The issue has forced its way to the forefront of the state's marquee U.S. Senate race. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is hoping to return to Congress with pointed attacks against Republican Sen. Jon Husted over the matter. Roughly $2.5 billion in state and local tax breaks over the last decade have prompted Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech companies to erect dozens of data centers across Ohio. That boom has spurred protests across the state , organized by local residents who are worried about the health, environmental, and financial impact of the structures. Brown has pinned the blame on Husted directly with ads airing widely across Ohio that call him "the face of data centers." "They're devouring our farmland, sucking up our water, and using our energy," Brown says in one recent video. A memo circulated by the National Republican Senatorial Committee in August and obtained by Politico described Brown's critiques as a big problem for Husted. "More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck," warns the Aug. 18 memo , which was shared with artificial intelligence companies. Husted has rebuffed these critiques by framing the construction of data centers as a local issue. More recently, he has said he wants to make sure that the companies building data centers pay for infrastructure costs, including energy. In a statement, Husted spokesperson Tom Evans reiterated that point, saying the senator believes "data centers should remain a local decision." It's not just costs that voters care about. An early-October opt-in survey of 1,650 Ohio adults by Ohio Northern University and SurveyUSA found that 55% were opposed to data center construction. About two-thirds had a negative opinion of data centers' impact on their community's environment, and about half said the same about their impact on quality of living. Opponents of data centers cite noise , air, and water pollution as a concern, according to a Gallup poll . Americans are more opposed to data centers in their area than nuclear power plants. The air pollution comes from gas turbines and diesel generators that have been linked to cardiovascular problems, asthma, and other health risks . Cooling system chemicals, heavy metals, and construction runoff can enter the water supply or rivers. "When they are fired up and powered by diesel, they emit a lot of air pollution like nitrogen oxide, and this pollutant can travel around the community and to those downwind," said Shaolei Ren, an electrical and computer engineering professor at the University of California-Riverside. In Page, residents in July voted out the mayor amid backlash over the Council's approval of the land sale for the data center. Opponents of data centers say it's a warning to candidates in the midterm elections who back new construction. Some residents in this picturesque town of about 7,000 people remain worried that the health effects could plague them if the project goes forward. Jan Boehme lives in a neighborhood close to the proposed site. From her front lawn with its "No Data Center" sign, she said she is concerned that a data center could become her new neighbor — and cause harms such as hearing loss. "We're against it," she said. "In this area, there are a lot of houses, and I'm concerned about all the noise." articles.title: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the “J5,” under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic. A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said “the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation” and they "wish him and his family the best.” Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran. Trump has vowed to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week. U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes. A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region . Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5. He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday. Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. “I call it accountability and long overdue,” Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30. Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a “purge” that will take years to rebuild. “He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.” ___ Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report. articles.title: 万科前三季营收1050亿元，净亏损239亿收窄14.5%，交付房3.4万套 | 财报见闻
articles.summary: 10月29日周四，万科A（000002.SZ）发布2026年第三季度报告。第三季度，公司实现营业收入348.30亿元，归母净亏损89.93亿元，亏损规模较上年同期收窄44.04%。 报告显示，万科前三季度实现营业收入1049.99亿元，同比下降34.94%；归母净亏损239.44亿元，较上年同期收窄14.53%。同期，公司完成119个项目、3.4万套住房交付，但合同销售金额同比下降48.2%，开发业务结算规模收缩仍对经营表现形成压力。 前三季度资产减值损失同比下降逾七成 第三季净亏收窄44% 万科前三季度亏损规模较上年同期有所收窄，但收入下降、开发业务毛利率处于低位的情况仍未改变。 财报显示，前三季度，万科归属于上市公司股东的净亏损为239.44亿元，较上年同期的280.16亿元减少40.72亿元，亏损同比收窄14.53%。第三季度，公司归母净亏损89.93亿元，较上年同期的160.69亿元减少70.76亿元，亏损同比收窄44.04%。 对于第三季度净亏将近90亿元，万科在报告中表示，主要原因是开发业务结算规模下滑、毛利率仍处低位等。 从收入端看，前三季度万科营业收入同比下降34.94%，第三季度同比下降37.88%，反映开发业务结算规模收缩仍在影响公司整体收入。 盈利能力方面，前三季度万科整体税前毛利率为6.6%，较上年同期下降3个百分点；其中，房地产开发业务税前毛利率为5.2%，同比下降2.6个百分点。公司前三季度毛利额为69.70亿元，较上年同期减少约85亿元。 另一方面，资产减值损失同比大幅下降，成为观察本期亏损变化的重要切入点。财报数据显示，前三季度万科资产减值损失为39.37亿元，同比下降72.54%，较上年同期减少约104亿元。 这意味着，尽管开发业务毛利额减少、毛利率下降，资产减值损失的显著减少仍对当期利润表现形成了重要影响。亏损收窄与主营业务盈利能力改善并非同一概念，仍需结合收入、毛利率及减值损失等指标综合判断。 扣非口径也显示出类似情况。前三季度，万科扣除非经常性损益后的净亏损为215.38亿元，同比收窄18.68%。这表明，公司亏损收窄并非仅由单一非经常性损益项目驱动，但开发业务结算规模和毛利率仍是影响业绩的关键因素。 前三季度销售520亿元，同比降约48% 开发业务销售表现仍面临压力，销售金额下降与结算规模收缩共同影响公司经营表现。 财报显示，前三季度，万科累计实现合同销售面积421.3万平方米，合同销售金额520.1亿元，同比分别下降45.6%和48.2%。 第三季度，公司实现合同销售面积128.3万平方米，合同销售金额162.1亿元，同比分别下降45.7%和48.3%。 截至9月底，万科合并报表范围内已售但尚未竣工结算的资源面积为893.3万平方米，对应合同金额约795.4亿元。这部分已售资源后续的竣工交付和结算进度，将影响未来相关收入的确认。 项目销售方面，万科继续加强重点项目管理和营销渠道建设。前三季度，公司12个首开项目均兑现投资承诺，整体首开去化率接近六成，其中宁波璞源隐秀项目首开去化率达到75%。 公司同时推进现房销售及存量产品去化。前三季度，万科年初现房实现销售75亿元，车位、商铺及办公产品销售58亿元，新媒体渠道获客成交金额近85亿元。 交付方面，前三季度万科完成119个项目、3.4万套住房交付。同期，公司实现新开工及复工计容面积159.6万平方米，占全年开复工计划的52.1%；竣工计容面积412.3万平方米，占全年计划竣工面积的55.4%。 盘活存量资源195亿元，回款39.2亿元，持续优化债务结构 在新增项目投资之外，万科继续通过存量资源盘活、大宗资产交易和融资优化等方式，推进资产负债结构调整。 财报显示，前三季度万科通过存量盘活累计优化和新增产能195亿元，实现存量盘活回款39.2亿元；大宗资产交易签约金额合计26.2亿元。同期，公司累计获取项目11个，权益计容建筑面积45.5万平方米，权益地价约30.7亿元。 这些举措反映出，万科在控制新增投资的同时，正尝试通过盘活现有资源、推动资产交易和回收资金，改善资金周转情况。不过，新增及优化产能、交易签约金额与实际现金回款属于不同统计口径，不能直接等同于当期收入或现金流入。 融资方面，截至三季度末，万科存量融资综合成本为2.86%，较年初下降17个基点。今年以来，大股东深圳市地铁集团累计向万科提供约45.2亿元股东借款。 截至报告期末，万科已有10只公开债券通过部分兑付、配套展期的方式完成风险缓释，涉及本金合计约180.7亿元。相关安排有助于调整债务偿付节奏，但部分债务通过展期等方式缓释，并不意味着相关债务已经全部偿还。 截至9月底，万科持有货币资金524.46亿元，有息负债合计3488.3亿元，资产负债率为78.0%，较上年末上升1.1个百分点。 现金流方面，前三季度万科经营活动产生的现金流量净额为-22.22亿元，较上年同期的-58.89亿元有所改善，经营性现金净流出同比收窄62.26%。 整体来看，万科经营性现金净流出收窄、存量融资成本下降，但货币资金较上年末减少，有息负债规模仍然较高。公司在财报中也表示，部分偿债能力财务指标尚未明显改善，化解债务风险的任务依然艰巨。 经营服务业务收入438亿元，租赁住宅与物流冷链保持增长 房地产开发业务之外，经营服务业务继续为万科提供收入补充。 前三季度，万科经营服务业务全口径收入438亿元，同比增长0.5%。其中，租赁住宅业务实现营业收入21亿元；商业开发与运营业务实现营业收入66.8亿元；万纬物流实现营业收入33.6亿元，同比增长5.6%。 截至9月底，万科旗下泊寓累计运营管理长租公寓21.36万间，其中已开业17.13万间，出租率为92.5%；商业业务整体出租率为93.1%。 物流业务方面，万纬物流前三季度冷链收入20.4亿元，同比增长21.9%；高标库收入13.2亿元，同比下降11.4%。截至9月底，其高标库稳定期出租率为90%，冷库稳定期库容使用率为79%。 经营服务业务整体收入保持稳定，冷链业务增长较快，但不同业务板块的表现存在差异。对于万科而言，经营服务业务能否进一步贡献稳定的经营现金流，以及存量资产盘活能否持续形成实际回款，仍是后续值得关注的方向。 万科在三季报中表示，下一阶段将继续聚焦化险和发展两大主题，推进城市与业务聚焦，提升产品与服务能力，并通过存量资源盘活、大宗资产交易、再融资及展期等方式，优化资产负债结构、有序缓释到期偿付压力。 从前三季度的财务数据看，万科归母净亏损同比收窄，但收入和销售规模仍在下降，开发业务毛利率处于低位。资产减值损失减少对亏损收窄形成重要影响，经营性现金流净流出收窄、融资成本下降则提供了部分缓冲。公司后续经营表现，仍取决于销售与交付、资产盘活回款以及债务偿付安排等多方面因素的变化。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 出口撑起增长，吉利再算利润账
articles.summary: 吉利的三季报刷新了其同期纪录。 10月29日，吉利汽车发布2026年第三季度财报。第三季度，公司实现收入990亿元，同比增长10%；核心归母净利润52.1亿元，同比增长32%，两项指标均创同期新高。 吉利汽车董事会副主席桂生悦在当天的业绩会上，将其称为“一份高压下的季报”。在他看来，过去三个月，吉利遭遇了近几年少有的严峻竞争，各条产品线都面临同质化产品的挑战。 桂生悦坦言，从内部角度看，“未来要让大家更满意、超出大家预期”，同时对未来发展有个更清晰思考。新车型密集推出，过去的畅销产品很快迎来同类竞争，意味着吉利需要不断补上新的产品优势。 第三季度，吉利出口32.34万辆，同比增加约21.14万辆；海外增长迅猛，出口占总销量的比例，也从去年同期的约14.7%升至39.8%。位居主流车企出海增速第一，且连续4个月月销超过10万辆，说明海外市场已经承担起更重的增长任务。 这份变化也影响着盈利。吉利在今年中报中，将出口产品与高端产品列为毛利较高的业务，并明确指出，它们的销量增加，加上规模协同和成本控制，共同推高了毛利率。 极氪把高端产品与海外需求接到了一起。据公司提供的业绩材料，前三季度极氪占集团销量的12.9%，收入占比达到31.3%。8月和9月，极氪出口均超过1.5万辆，占品牌当月销量四成以上。这个收入权重较高的品牌，正在把更多产品卖到海外。 吉利前三季度的新能源出口已达48.4万辆，约占海外销量六成。过去几年为新能源和高端化开发的产品，有了国内之外的市场来承接，前期投入也有机会在更多销量上获得回报。 前三季度，吉利总收入达2726亿元，同比增长13%；核心归母净利润累计149亿元，同比增长41%，增速高于收入。同期毛利率达18%，同比提升1.5个百分点。销售组合改善的效果，已经体现在整体盈利中。 研发是理解这份利润表的另一处关键。 吉利汽车集团CFO戴永在业绩会上表示，前三季度研发投入约149亿元，“研发投入与去年同期基本持平”。但当期研发投入的费用化比例，已经从去年同期的32.1%提高至40.7%，上升8.6个百分点。 一笔研发支出，直接费用化的部分会计入当期损益；符合条件、予以资本化的部分，则在以后逐步摊销。费用化比例提高，意味着本期研发投入中有更多成本由当期利润承担。 这也是核心归母净利润增长41%值得注意的地方：当期研发投入没有明显增加，直接计入损益的比例却更高，经营仍然实现了增长。高毛利产品和市场的占比提高，为持续投入提供了支撑；桂生悦所谈到的同质化竞争，又要求这些投入继续转化为产品差异。 海外的毛利空间要维持下去，吉利还得把账算到当地工厂里。 在回应出口政策和贸易环境变化时，吉利汽车控股行政总裁、吉利汽车集团CEO淦家阅谈到了本地化生产，他指出，欧洲当地成本可能明显高于国内，需要供应商随整车企业共同出海，也要与海外供应商和当地生产资源合作。 本地化能让产品更靠近市场，却也意味着生产成本要重新核算。随着当地制造的比重提高，吉利需要把在中国形成的供应链效率带过去，再与当地的生产条件衔接。 淦家阅特别提到，一些当地产能“有可能折旧已经基本上也折得差不多了”，可以通过专用设备改造，控制导入新产品的成本。 新建工厂需要先投入厂房、设备和配套，再靠之后的销量逐步消化；在既有工厂导入新车型，则有机会把新增投入更多集中在产线改造和产品适配上。工厂原有的用工、供应商体系也可以继续使用，减少从头组织生产的成本。 这些改造和适配投入，仍需要投产后的销量来分摊。管理层谈到的合作，因而既是争取进入市场的速度，也是在控制扩张所需的投入。 7月公布的吉利汽车与福特合作方案，拟利用西班牙瓦伦西亚现有工厂生产双方车型，并分摊开发成本；领克则按9月公布的协议，自2027年1月起由沃尔沃担任欧洲独家分销商，接入其既有销售和服务网络。 吉利汽车控股董事会主席安聪慧在会上介绍了欧盟本地化布局的整体进度：产品验证、工厂技术改造和本地供应链布局正在推进，预计2027年会有重要产品在欧盟当地工厂投产。借助合作伙伴的产能、用工和供应链，尽快形成规模，是管理层明确提出的路径。 对于更近的四季度，桂生悦认为，三季度推出的产品，其效果还将进一步体现。他在业绩会上给出了明确预期：“我相信我们的第四季度，我们一定还是会比第三季度更加好的。” 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.summary: 作者 | 周智宇 利润刚回到百亿元，比亚迪又加大了投入。 10月29日披露的三季报显示，比亚迪第三季度营收2214.88亿元，同比增长13.59%；归母净利润100.20亿元，同比增长28.08%；扣非归母净利润86.30亿元，同比增长25.25%。营收、归母净利润分别环比增长13.82%、21.58%。 前三季度，比亚迪营收5663.04亿元，与去年同期基本持平，归母净利润223.45亿元，同比下降4.24%。 同一季度，比亚迪购建固定资产、无形资产和其他长期资产支付的现金达到426.76亿元，环比增长88.49%，几乎赶上整个上半年的447.03亿元。前三季度累计支出仍比去年同期低约24%，但进入三季度，付款明显加快了。上半年披露的分部资本性支出中，汽车及相关业务占96.4%，投入重心仍在汽车制造体系。 闪充车型的扩产，是其中一条可以追溯的线索。6月股东大会上，比亚迪董事长王传福解释，第二代刀片电池正处于新旧产线切换期，产能爬坡跟不上订单。华尔街见闻当时从供应链方面了解到，由于工艺调整，预计三季度高端车型的产能才会有所缓解。 比亚迪有庞大的生产规模，但新电池、新车型仍要经历设备改造和产线磨合。中报披露，上半年约132亿元净值的机器设备从固定资产转入在建工程，反映出部分既有设备重新进入建设、改造过程。对于自制电池的比亚迪，新技术换代的投入会一直延伸到电芯生产环节。 西咸动力电池基地就覆盖了电芯、电池包等生产环节，从3月试生产走到9月底全面建成投产。此前对三季度供给缓解的预期，也开始得到车型销量的印证：搭载新技术的大唐，8月销量达到11010辆。 三季度，比亚迪总销量132.31万辆，环比增长近两成。纯电乘用车贡献了绝大部分增量，环比多卖约20.54万辆，占乘用车新增销量的九成五以上。公司在9月投关记录中，将此前销量回升主要归因于以闪充系列为代表的新车型上市。这20.54万辆中也有其他车型和出口的贡献。 随新车一起铺开的，还有闪充站。6月底，比亚迪建成7018座闪充站，到8月28日增至1万座。承建方中交设计的半年报，也披露了中标比亚迪站中站闪充项目华东、华北区域建设的情况。闪充要成为日常用车中可兑现的卖点，车主就得找到足够方便的站点。工厂之外，充电设备、安装施工也在花钱。 海外的支出同样不能忽略。三季度，比亚迪出口55.07万辆，出口同比增量超过公司总销量的同比增量。卖到海外的车越来越多，本地工厂却还没有建完。巴西卡马萨里基地虽已开始组装汽车，比亚迪9月仍披露，其焊装、涂装和冲压工厂处于建设最后阶段。9月3日，印尼苏邦工厂也正式开业，设计年产能15万辆。 三季度归母利润环比增加17.79亿元，非经常性损益净额就增加了13.74亿元，占归母利润环比增量的约77%，金融资产相关损益由亏转盈是重要来源。扣非归母净利润环比只增长4.92%。 包含电子等业务在内的集团毛利率，也从二季度的18.88%降至18.01%。与此同时，在建工程余额升至791.81亿元，较6月底增加101.91亿元。这些资产后续转固，会陆续进入折旧成本。在利润率承压时，比亚迪需要更大的产销规模来摊薄新增固定成本。 扩大的销售规模，也在占用更多周转资金。季报将存货、应收账款较年初增加主要归因于海外业务和备货需求。仅第三季度，两项余额就分别增加315.87亿元和63.46亿元。 比亚迪仍在加快建设付款，押注新技术和海外市场能够带来持续需求。国内更新电池产线，海外补齐制造工序，这套扩张路径也让它与未来几年的销售绑得更紧。产能建起来以后，就需要长期稳定的订单来消化。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 国产新作《影之刃零》发售登顶全球畅销榜！评分超《黑神话：悟空》，冯骥发声力挺，国产3A不再孤军
articles.summary: 10月29日，《影之刃零》游戏发售不足一小时，Steam同时在线人数已突破30万，热度持续攀升。截至13时30分，第三方平台SteamDB监测显示，《影之刃零》发售首日Steam同时在线峰值站上43万人，稳居Steam全球畅销榜第一位。 作为对照，发售满800天的《黑神话：悟空》，两年前首发一小时后Steam同时在线人数突破100万。相较之下，对于一款没有“西游记”这样强大IP（具有商业价值的创意内容或品牌）加持的国产新作，《影之刃零》的数据已经难能可贵。而游戏科学创始人、《黑神话：悟空》制作人冯骥29日的发声力挺，更加点燃市场情绪，“黑神话悟空 影之刃零”相关词条也随之登上微博热搜。 10月29日凌晨，灵游坊创始人兼CEO（首席执行官）、《影之刃零》制作人梁其伟更新了一条微信朋友圈，文案只有简短一句话：“一个疯狂星期四。”配图中，PS5的屏幕定格在游戏更新界面。前一日，梁其伟发布长文复盘从20年前独立游戏《雨血：死镇》起步，一路走到3A（高成本、高体量、高质量）单机开发的漫长历程。 冯骥那句“桃李不言，功不唐捐”，或许正是这群创作者最好的注脚。从梁其伟二十年前落笔《雨血》，到如今《影之刃零》利刃出鞘，国产买断单机早已不是单枪匹马的冒险。国产3A大作不再孤军，但高投入长周期的考验仍横亘在前：这条以热爱铺就的道路，才刚刚从一则“神话”，迈入一场漫长的集体试炼。 冯骥发文力挺：和梁其伟“殊途同归” 不同于自带国民认知基础的西游IP，《影之刃零》走原创“功夫朋克”武侠路线，把港式功夫、传统武术、机械改造、平行世界幻想融合在自研的“影境”世界观之中。在国产买断单机赛道，这是继《黑神话：悟空》之后，又一款收获全球主流游戏媒体认可的作品。 发售前夜，市场热度已经率先发酵。10月27日，《影之刃零》登顶Steam全球热销榜。第三方市场分析机构Alinea Analytics估算，10月27日至28日，其在Steam、PS5双平台的累计预购量约85万份，预购收入折合人民币约2.87亿元。口碑层面，《影之刃零》PC版在海外游戏评分汇总网站Metacritic拿到88分媒体均分，超过了《黑神话：悟空》的81分。国际知名游戏媒体IGN给出9分评价。 《影之刃零》的爆火，也把行业话题推向更深一层：国产单机不再依靠单一爆款孤证，一批不同风格、不同体量的工作室集中进场，赛道正在从“0到1”的突破阶段，迈向“1到N”的持续验证。 为业界关注的是，冯骥在最新发声中力挺梁其伟，也道出了国产单机创作者共同面对的机遇与困境。 “单机游戏，并非更高级的游戏。选择做单机的人，大约只是因为在自由的空闲时间里，更多在玩单机。”冯骥在29日的最新发文中表示，如果把人比作大模型，一路接收的语料、标注与反馈，塑造了创作者的审美与同理心，决定创作者擅长输出什么，“说的好听点，叫热爱；说的俗一点，就是对做的事更熟悉，仅此而已”。 多年前，冯骥和梁其伟都还是创业新人，同样深耕手游赛道，两人曾围坐在一起，认真讨论游戏设计理论，思索叙事、战斗、付费体系如何结合。彼时的他们，未曾预料到多年之后，两人会先后放下手游业务，押注周期漫长、风险极高的买断制单机。 不仅仅是冯骥，《影之刃零》的特别鸣谢名单里，腾讯马晓轶、游戏科学冯骥、米哈游刘伟、库洛游戏李松伦、英雄游戏吴旦、心动网络黄一孟等国内游戏行业核心人物悉数在列，同时还包含索尼吉田修平、Tim Sweeney、金亨泰等海外行业知名人士。 尽管鸣谢名单无法直接等同于商业合作协议，但这份跨厂商、跨赛道、跨国界的行业联结，勾勒出国产3A赛道一个新变化：单机创作不再是孤立的孤军奋战，行业内部正在形成相互理解、彼此托举的生态氛围。 冯骥也在转发与评论中持续给其他国产单机团队打气。《归唐》预告片放出时，冯骥曾主动转发支持，制作人胡志鹏留言致谢：“是你们让我们更坚定。”这种同行之间的惺惺相惜，在高风险的3A赛道更具特殊意义。 当然，关于3A游戏高风险高投入的拷问，也是资本层面最关心的问题。 数字化内容营销服务商DataEye研究院院长刘尊在接受《每日经济新闻》记者采访时分析，《黑神话：悟空》依托西游IP，具备极低的全球认知门槛，同时叠加国产3A“首款突破者”带来的情绪红利，不仅能打动主机核心玩家，也将大量原本尚未接触买断游戏的泛用户拉入市场；而《影之刃零》作为原创武侠IP，没有天然的IP红利，核心吸引力落在战斗手感与独特美学，高度依赖口碑发酵，其出海受众也集中在动作游戏核心圈层，很难像西游IP那样击穿全球大众市场。 这两条截然不同的商业化路径，也代表国产3A出海的两条分支：国民神话IP走大众化路线，原创动作IP深耕垂直硬核玩家。 事实上，灵游坊选择砍掉其余在研项目，全部押注《影之刃零》，是中小工作室布局3A最极致、也是风险最高的选择。在刘尊看来，集中全部资源押注单一项目，优势在于可以集中有限人力守住品质底线，避免多项目并行带来的品质妥协；同时跳出已经高度“内卷”、边际收益持续下滑的手游赛道，抓住单机赛道关注度抬升的窗口，拿到平台、产业资本、文创政策的配套资源。 但他同时指出，这一选择背后风险同样致命：3A项目研发周期普遍3至5年，砍掉其他产品线，意味着团队失去稳定现金流对冲，高度依赖外部持续融资；一旦项目延期、口碑不及预期，资金链压力会瞬间爆发。 赛道扩容：国产单机从爆款个案走向集体试炼 《影之刃零》的登场，不是孤立事件。在它身后，一条由不同风格工作室组成的国产动作单机矩阵正在成型，赛道正在告别“等待下一个黑神话”的单一叙事。 一批批体量不同、背景各异的团队陆续拿出实机与预告片，题材覆盖末世传说、西部民俗、明末武侠、晚唐历史、上古神话，玩法也在类魂框架之外寻找差异化。 成都蛇夫座日蚀边缘工作室的《湮灭之潮》，把亚瑟王传说置于末世伦敦，主打骑士协同作战；上海暗星科技的《达巴：水痕之地》扎根西部民俗幻想，聚焦双形态武器立体攻防；钛核网络延续《暗影火炬城》积累，推出《动物朋克》；铃空游戏的《昭和米国物语》以混搭复古流行文化，打造差异化的荒诞叙事。 大厂体系内同样有新项目落地：网易雷火临安24工作室的《归唐》，将镜头对准晚唐敦煌，走写实历史叙事路线；烛龙在《古剑奇谭》IP基础上推出新作《古剑》，转向动作RPG（角色扮演游戏）开发；游戏科学也已经公布《黑神话：钟馗》，延续神话买断制路线。 值得一提的是，供给快速增加，并不等于赛道已经跑通常态化盈利。 在业内人士看来，国产3A大作已跨过从无到有的门槛，但距离稳定闭环的生意尚有距离。 刘尊认为，成本回报结构的错配，是摆在所有团队面前最大的卡点。大型3A投入动辄数亿元，回本往往需要百万级甚至千万级销量，能够触达这个门槛的国产作品目前寥寥无几；大量腰部项目定价受国区天花板约束，几万到几十万份的销量，利润微薄，很难长期支撑工业化团队。同时，赛道已经出现同质化倾向，东方神话、武侠+ARPG（动作角色扮演游戏）的组合扎堆，海外市场对东方题材的新鲜感存在消耗，缺少题材、玩法、系统层面的创新。除此之外，国内玩家长期习惯手游免费模式，买断用户基本盘有限；多数团队只擅长一次性交付线性单机，缺少DLC（可下载内容）、MOD（模组）生态、持续内容运营能力，发售之后收入快速衰减，难以依靠存量持续造血。叠加版号、档期竞争、海外本地化折扣等变量，整条赛道的不确定性依旧很高。 而在社交平台上，冯骥则从创作者视角，将漫长的开发过程类比为人的训练过程：“对我们的碳基大脑而言，不断答题，不断交卷，不断被真实世界反馈，虽然训练周期比硅基漫长得多，却依然是提升‘模型能力’最有效的办法。这个世界始终存在着某种宏大的公平。桃李不言，功不唐捐。”在他看来，梁其伟和团队用二十年持续回答同一个命题，《影之刃零》就是这份答卷。 资本市场正在持续观察这条赛道的演化逻辑：国产3A的价值，早已不止单款游戏的销售收入，它承载着国产游戏工业化能力验证、文化出海、IP长线开发的巨大想象空间。 本文来源： 每日经济新闻 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
